lesson_title: Describe Image: Planning, Fluency, Pronunciation, and Timed Practice

overview.what_it_is: Describe Image is a PTE Academic speaking task in which the test taker studies an academic image, quickly identifies its main message and important details, and delivers a clear, logically organized spoken description. Images may include graphs, charts, tables, maps, diagrams, photographs, or other visual information.

format_facts.label: Preparation time
format_facts.value: 25 seconds to inspect the image and prepare brief speaking notes.

format_facts.label: Speaking time
format_facts.value: 40 seconds to record the spoken description.

format_facts.label: Response mode
format_facts.value: The response is spoken into a microphone and should begin promptly after recording starts.

format_facts.label: Typical image types
format_facts.value: Line graphs, bar charts, pie charts, tables, maps, processes, diagrams, and photographs.

format_facts.label: Primary objective
format_facts.value: Communicate the image's overall message and its most significant supporting details clearly and fluently.

scoring_factors.name: Content
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: How accurately and sufficiently the response communicates the main topic, important features, relationships, figures, trends, contrasts, or stages shown in the image.

scoring_factors.name: Oral fluency
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: How smoothly and naturally the response is delivered, including rhythm, phrasing, pace, continuity, and control of pauses, repetitions, hesitations, and false starts.

scoring_factors.name: Pronunciation
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: How clearly sounds, words, syllable stress, sentence stress, and intonation are produced so that the response is easy to understand.

critical_rules: Use the 25 seconds to identify the image type, topic, labels, units, major features, and a logical speaking order rather than writing complete sentences.
Begin with an overview that identifies what the image shows before giving individual figures or visual details.
Select the most important information; do not attempt to mention every number, label, object, or category.
Support general statements with accurate figures, categories, positions, or visible evidence whenever these are available.
Choose verb tense from the image's time information: use present forms for timeless or current information and past forms for completed historical periods.
Keep speaking in connected phrases at a controlled pace; a simpler continuous answer is usually clearer than an ambitious answer filled with pauses and self-corrections.
Stress key nouns, adjectives, numbers, and contrast words rather than articles, prepositions, and other small grammatical words.
Finish with a short overall observation when time permits, but do not sacrifice important content to force a memorized conclusion.

learning_goals: Explain the preparation and speaking times for the Describe Image item type.
Identify the main topic and communication purpose of a graph, chart, table, map, diagram, or photograph.
Create a usable six-part plan within 25 seconds using keywords rather than complete sentences.
Organize a spoken response from overview to major details and final observation.
Select high-value information such as the highest figure, lowest figure, dominant category, major trend, exception, contrast, or process stage.
Use suitable language for quantities, comparisons, proportions, trends, spatial relationships, and visual contrast.
Choose an appropriate tense by checking the dates or time periods shown in the image.
Speak for approximately 35 to 40 seconds without excessive hesitation, repetition, or restarting.
Use word stress, sentence stress, pausing, and intonation to make important information easy to follow.
Evaluate a recorded response using a checklist covering content, organization, fluency, pronunciation, grammar, and vocabulary.

core_method.name: SCAN–PLAN–SPEAK
core_method.summary: Use the preparation time to scan the image for its structure and main message, reduce the visual information to a small set of speaking notes, and deliver those notes in a predictable order: overview, major features, supporting evidence, and final observation.

steps.detail: Name the image type and determine the broad topic. Ask: Is this a line graph, bar chart, pie chart, table, map, process, diagram, or photograph, and what subject does it present?
Read the title, axes, legends, labels, dates, units, categories, locations, arrows, and captions. Confirm what each visual element represents before selecting details.
Choose three or four high-value features, such as the highest and lowest values, overall direction, largest contrast, unusual exception, dominant section, or main stages.
Arrange the selected features logically. Use overview first, then move from largest to smallest, left to right, past to present, general to specific, or first stage to final stage.
Write only keywords, numbers, comparison signs, tense reminders, and useful verbs. Avoid drafting complete sentences because this consumes preparation time.
Start promptly, speak in meaningful phrases, emphasize key information, use linking expressions, and continue steadily until the description is complete.
End with a brief summary of the dominant pattern, contrast, outcome, or overall impression when sufficient time remains.

core_method.formula: Overview sentence + major feature 1 with evidence + major feature 2 with evidence + comparison, trend, contrast, or exception + brief overall observation

techniques.name: Six-note preparation grid
techniques.purpose: Convert a complex image into a compact plan that can be prepared within 25 seconds.
how_to: Write the image type in one or two words.
Write the main topic or title.
Note the most important labels, groups, stages, or locations.
Record the unit of measurement or scale.
Mark the highest, lowest, largest, smallest, first, or final feature.
Add one trend, comparison, contrast, exception, or overall result.
techniques.example: Line graph | city transport | bus/train/bicycle | millions | train highest 2023 | cycling rises steadily
techniques.why_it_matters: The grid gives the response enough structure and content without requiring full-sentence planning.
techniques.common_error: Writing a complete introduction during preparation and then having too little time to inspect the remaining data.

techniques.name: Overview before numbers
techniques.purpose: Establish the image's subject and main message before presenting detailed evidence.
how_to: Name the visual type.
State the topic or variables being compared.
Mention the time period or location when relevant.
Add the dominant pattern if it is immediately clear.
techniques.example: The line graph compares the use of three forms of public transport in a city between 2018 and 2023, and it shows an overall rise in train and bicycle use.
techniques.why_it_matters: A clear overview helps the listener understand how later figures and comparisons fit together.
techniques.common_error: Beginning with an isolated number such as 'Twenty-five percent' without explaining what the figure represents.

techniques.name: Feature selection
techniques.purpose: Focus the response on information that contributes most strongly to an accurate description.
how_to: Look for the highest and lowest values.
Identify the strongest increase, decrease, or fluctuation.
Notice the largest difference between categories.
Find any exception that does not follow the general pattern.
Ignore minor values when they do not change the main interpretation.
techniques.example: In a chart with eight categories, mention the dominant category, the smallest category, and the closest comparison rather than reading all eight percentages.
techniques.why_it_matters: Forty seconds is not enough to report every detail, so prioritization protects both content quality and fluency.
techniques.common_error: Reading every value in order and failing to communicate the overall pattern.

techniques.name: Safe approximation
techniques.purpose: Describe figures accurately when exact values are difficult to read or unnecessary.
how_to: Use 'approximately' or 'about' for values near a visible mark.
Use 'just over' when a point is slightly above a marked value.
Use 'just under' when a point is slightly below a marked value.
Use 'nearly' when a value approaches a clear total or benchmark.
Avoid inventing a precise figure when the scale is unclear.
techniques.example: The figure rose to approximately 60 percent, while the second category remained just under 40 percent.
techniques.why_it_matters: Responsible approximation maintains accuracy and allows smoother delivery.
techniques.common_error: Guessing an exact number and presenting it confidently even though the chart does not clearly support it.

techniques.name: Logical visual route
techniques.purpose: Prevent random movement around the image and make the spoken description easy to follow.
how_to: For line graphs, move through time or compare the most important lines.
For bar charts, move from the highest bar to the lowest or compare related groups.
For pie charts, begin with the largest segment and move toward smaller segments.
For tables, compare rows or columns using one consistent direction.
For photographs and maps, move from foreground to background, left to right, or central feature to surrounding details.
techniques.example: The largest segment is housing at 40 percent, followed by food at 25 percent, while transport and entertainment account for smaller shares.
techniques.why_it_matters: A consistent route reduces hesitation and improves oral organization.
techniques.common_error: Jumping repeatedly between unrelated areas of the image as new details are noticed.

techniques.name: Tense from visual time
techniques.purpose: Maintain grammatical consistency and accurately place information in time.
how_to: Use the simple present when the image presents a general relationship or has no completed historical period.
Use the simple past for figures tied to completed years or past periods.
Use present forms when describing what the image visually shows, such as 'the chart illustrates.'
Use future language only when the image explicitly shows predictions or projections.
Keep the chosen tense consistent across related details.
techniques.example: The chart illustrates population change, and the population increased from 2 million in 2010 to 3 million in 2020.
techniques.why_it_matters: Correct tense makes the timeline clear and prevents avoidable grammar errors.
techniques.common_error: Switching randomly between present and past while describing the same historical data.

techniques.name: Stress the information words
techniques.purpose: Make the main message, contrasts, and figures easier for the listener to recognize.
how_to: Stress important nouns such as 'population,' 'transport,' and 'revenue.'
Stress descriptive adjectives and adverbs such as 'highest,' 'sharp,' and 'gradually.'
Stress important numbers, dates, percentages, and units.
Stress contrast markers such as 'however,' 'whereas,' and 'in contrast.'
Reduce stress on articles, auxiliary verbs, and prepositions unless they express a contrast.
techniques.example: TRAIN use rose SHARPLY to SIXTY percent, whereas BUS use remained STABLE.
techniques.why_it_matters: English rhythm depends on prominent information words, and correct sentence stress supports both clarity and fluency.
techniques.common_error: Giving every word equal stress, which makes the response sound mechanical and hides the important information.

techniques.name: Fluency recovery
techniques.purpose: Continue speaking effectively after a small mistake or forgotten detail.
how_to: Correct only errors that seriously change the meaning.
Use a neutral linker such as 'In addition' or 'Turning to the next category' to restart the flow.
Replace a forgotten precise word with a simpler accurate phrase.
Move to the next planned feature instead of repeating the previous sentence.
Maintain a calm, moderate speaking rate after the interruption.
techniques.example: The rate increased in 2020—more specifically, it reached about 45 percent—and then remained stable.
techniques.why_it_matters: Small errors are less damaging than long silences, repeated restarts, or loss of rhythm.
techniques.common_error: Stopping, apologizing, and beginning the entire response again.

worked_examples.title: Line graph: Urban transport use
worked_examples.input: A line graph compares the number of city residents using buses, trains, and bicycles from 2018 to 2023. Bus use falls from 55 million to 42 million journeys. Train use rises from 40 million to 68 million. Bicycle use increases steadily from 15 million to 35 million.
worked_examples.decoding: The image contains three transport categories, a six-year historical period, and journeys measured in millions. The strongest features are the rise in train use, the decline in bus use, and the steady growth of cycling.
worked_examples.plan: Line graph; urban transport; 2018–2023; millions; trains 40→68 highest; buses 55→42 down; bicycles 15→35 steady; overall shift.
worked_examples.model_answer: The line graph compares the number of journeys made by bus, train, and bicycle in a city between 2018 and 2023. Overall, train and bicycle use increased, whereas bus travel declined. Train journeys rose strongly from about 40 million in 2018 to 68 million in 2023, making trains the most widely used option by the end of the period. In contrast, bus use fell from 55 million to approximately 42 million. Bicycle journeys remained the least common, but they increased steadily from 15 million to 35 million. Overall, the graph indicates a clear shift away from buses.

annotations.comment: Identifies the image type, categories, location, and historical period.
Summarizes the main directions before presenting individual figures.
Uses beginning and ending values to support the description of each trend.
Uses 'whereas' and 'in contrast' to separate rising and falling patterns.
Interprets the combined pattern without introducing unsupported information.

worked_examples.title: Bar chart: Renewable electricity by country
worked_examples.input: A bar chart shows the percentage of electricity produced from renewable sources in five countries. Norway records 72 percent, New Zealand 58 percent, Canada 41 percent, Australia 32 percent, and Japan 18 percent.
worked_examples.decoding: The chart compares five countries using percentages. Norway is clearly the highest, Japan is the lowest, and New Zealand ranks second. The gap between the highest and lowest countries is 54 percentage points.
worked_examples.plan: Bar chart; renewable electricity; percentages; Norway 72 highest; NZ 58; Canada 41; Australia 32; Japan 18 lowest; 54-point gap.
worked_examples.model_answer: The bar chart compares the proportion of electricity generated from renewable sources in five countries. Norway has the highest figure at 72 percent, followed by New Zealand at 58 percent. Canada occupies the middle position, producing 41 percent of its electricity from renewable energy. Australia records a lower share of 32 percent, while Japan has the smallest proportion at only 18 percent. The difference between Norway and Japan is therefore substantial, at 54 percentage points. Overall, the chart shows considerable variation among the countries, with the two leading nations well ahead of the remaining three.

annotations.comment: The first sentence defines exactly what the percentages represent.
The response follows a highest-to-lowest route, which is easy to track.
Expressions such as 'followed by,' 'middle position,' and 'smallest proportion' avoid repetitive number listing.
The 54-point gap is a relevant comparison derived directly from the supplied values.
The conclusion summarizes variation without speculating about causes.

worked_examples.title: Pie chart: Monthly household expenditure
worked_examples.input: A pie chart presents household spending by category. Housing accounts for 38 percent, food 24 percent, transport 16 percent, utilities 12 percent, and recreation 10 percent.
worked_examples.decoding: The chart shows proportions of a whole. Housing is the dominant category, recreation is the smallest, and housing plus food represents 62 percent of total spending.
worked_examples.plan: Pie chart; household budget; housing 38 largest; food 24; transport 16; utilities 12; recreation 10 smallest; housing+food 62.
worked_examples.model_answer: The pie chart illustrates how a household distributes its monthly expenditure across five categories. Housing represents the largest share at 38 percent, while food is the second-largest expense at 24 percent. Together, these two essential categories account for 62 percent of the total budget. Transport makes up a further 16 percent, followed by utilities at 12 percent. Recreation receives the smallest allocation, at only 10 percent. Overall, the household spends almost two-thirds of its budget on housing and food, whereas less than one-quarter is allocated to utilities and recreation combined.

annotations.comment: The answer begins with the largest segment and moves toward smaller ones.
Uses 'represents,' 'accounts for,' 'makes up,' and 'allocation' to describe shares.
Combines housing and food to communicate a more meaningful overall pattern.
'Almost two-thirds' restates 62 percent naturally without changing the meaning.
The final sentence contrasts essential expenses with smaller categories.

worked_examples.title: Table: University enrolment by faculty
worked_examples.input: A table lists student enrolment in four university faculties in 2022 and 2025. Engineering rises from 2,400 to 3,100 students, Business from 3,000 to 3,300, Science from 2,800 to 2,750, and Arts from 2,200 to 2,500.
worked_examples.decoding: The table compares four faculties across two completed years. Engineering shows the largest increase, Business has the highest total in 2025, Science declines slightly, and Arts grows moderately.
worked_examples.plan: Table; enrolment; 2022 vs 2025; students; Business 3300 highest final; Engineering +700 biggest rise; Science -50 exception; Arts +300.
worked_examples.model_answer: The table compares student enrolment in four university faculties in 2022 and 2025. Business had the highest enrolment in 2025, increasing slightly from 3,000 to 3,300 students. Engineering experienced the largest growth, rising by 700 students from 2,400 to 3,100. Arts also increased, from 2,200 to 2,500 students. Science was the only faculty to record a decline, although the change was small, falling from 2,800 to 2,750. Overall, enrolment grew in three of the four faculties, with Engineering showing the most significant expansion.

annotations.comment: The response consistently uses the past tense because both years are completed historical periods.
It highlights the highest final total, largest increase, and only decline.
Science is identified as the sole category moving against the general pattern.
Changes are supported with exact starting and ending figures.
The final statement summarizes the direction across all four faculties.

worked_examples.title: Photograph: Traditional and modern architecture
worked_examples.input: A photograph shows an old two-storey stone building on the left and a tall modern glass building on the right. The older building has a rough grey surface, small windows, and classical decorative features. The newer building has a smooth reflective exterior, many large windows, and a simple geometric design. People and trees appear in the foreground.
worked_examples.decoding: The main purpose is visual contrast. Useful comparison areas are age, height, materials, surface, windows, style, and position. Minor foreground details can be mentioned after the central contrast.
worked_examples.plan: Photo; architecture contrast; old left vs modern right; stone/glass; low/tall; rough/smooth; classical/geometric; people and trees foreground.
worked_examples.model_answer: The photograph contrasts two very different styles of architecture. On the left, there is an older two-storey building constructed from grey stone. It has a rough exterior, relatively small windows, and several classical decorative features. In contrast, the building on the right is much taller and has a modern glass surface that appears smooth and reflective. Its large windows and simple geometric shape give it a contemporary appearance. Several people and trees can also be seen in the foreground. Overall, the image emphasizes the contrast between traditional stone architecture and modern urban design.

annotations.comment: The response immediately identifies the photograph's central relationship.
It describes the left side first and then the right side.
Older and modern, rough and smooth, small and large, and classical and contemporary create clear comparisons.
Materials, windows, height, and surface provide visible evidence for the contrast.
People and trees are included only after the main subject has been fully described.

worked_examples.title: Process diagram: Recycling plastic bottles
worked_examples.input: A process diagram shows six stages: used bottles are placed in recycling bins, collected by truck, sorted at a facility, crushed and washed, converted into plastic pellets, and manufactured into new products.
worked_examples.decoding: The image is a linear process with six sequential stages. The response should describe the starting point, major transformations, and final outcome using sequencing expressions and passive structures.
worked_examples.plan: Process; plastic recycling; bins → truck → sorting → crush/wash → pellets → new goods; six stages; linear cycle.
worked_examples.model_answer: The diagram illustrates a six-stage process for recycling used plastic bottles. First, consumers place the bottles in designated recycling bins, after which they are collected and transported by truck to a processing facility. At the facility, recyclable bottles are separated from unsuitable material. They are then crushed into smaller pieces and thoroughly washed. Next, the clean plastic is processed into pellets, which provide the raw material for manufacturing. In the final stage, these pellets are transformed into new plastic products. Overall, the diagram shows how discarded bottles are collected, processed, and returned to productive use.

annotations.comment: Names the process and states the total number of stages.
Uses 'first,' 'after which,' 'then,' 'next,' and 'in the final stage' to guide the listener.
Structures such as 'are collected' and 'are transformed' focus attention on the process rather than the actor.
The answer explains how bottles change into pieces, pellets, and new products.
Summarizes the complete movement from waste to reuse.

Use when several categories, groups, countries, or periods are represented by bars.

common_mistakes.mistake: Starting with numbers before identifying the topic.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The listener cannot easily understand what the figures represent, and the response lacks a clear structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Begin with one overview sentence naming the image type, topic, variables, and time period when relevant.

common_mistakes.mistake: Attempting to report every visible value.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The response becomes a rushed list, important patterns are hidden, and fluency usually deteriorates.
common_mistakes.fix: Select the highest, lowest, dominant trend, strongest contrast, and one useful supporting detail.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a memorized template without adapting it to the image.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Generic language consumes speaking time and may fail to communicate meaningful image content.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a flexible structure but insert specific labels, relationships, figures, stages, or visible features from the image.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving unsupported explanations or personal opinions.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Speculation replaces accurate description and can introduce information that is not shown.
common_mistakes.fix: Describe only what the image displays or what can be safely inferred from direct visual relationships.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing the wrong tense or changing tense repeatedly.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The timeline becomes unclear and grammar control weakens.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the dates during preparation and mark a tense reminder such as 'past,' 'present,' or 'projection.'

common_mistakes.mistake: Speaking too quickly to include more details.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Pronunciation becomes less clear, word endings disappear, and the rhythm may sound unnatural.
common_mistakes.fix: Use fewer details, speak at a moderate rate, and pause briefly between meaningful phrases.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The response sounds fragmented and weakens oral fluency.
common_mistakes.fix: Group words into sense units, such as 'from 2018 to 2023' or 'the largest category at 45 percent.'

common_mistakes.mistake: Restarting the whole response after a minor error.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Restarting wastes time and creates repetitions and false starts.
common_mistakes.fix: Correct the word briefly when necessary and continue with the next planned feature.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving equal stress to every word.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Important numbers, categories, and contrasts are difficult to recognize.
common_mistakes.fix: Emphasize content words, figures, and contrast markers while reducing small grammatical words.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The most important content may become difficult to understand.
common_mistakes.fix: During preparation, silently rehearse difficult category names, dates, percentages, and measurement units.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing a photograph as if it were a statistical chart.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The response may use unsuitable language and fail to explain visible objects, positions, or contrasts.
common_mistakes.fix: For photographs, identify the main subject, organize details spatially, and describe visible contrasts and relationships.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The response may not contain enough development or supporting information.
common_mistakes.fix: Prepare at least four speaking units: overview, major feature one, major feature two, and an overall comparison or conclusion.

time_budget.focus: Review the 25-second preparation time, 40-second response time, image types, scoring factors, and response structure.
Identify titles, axes, labels, legends, units, dates, categories, spatial features, and process arrows.
Reduce five different images to six short notes each without writing complete sentences.
Practise overview-first descriptions using highest, lowest, trend, contrast, and exception language.
Use spatial organization for photographs and sequencing language for diagrams.
Practise sense groups, key-word stress, number pronunciation, linking, and controlled pace.
Complete three full tasks using exactly 25 seconds of preparation and up to 40 seconds of speaking.
Use a checklist to identify one content strength, one delivery strength, and one priority for improvement.

drills.name: Twenty-five-second scan
drills.instructions: Display an unfamiliar image for exactly 25 seconds. Write only six notes: type, topic, labels, unit, major feature, and trend or contrast. Stop writing when time ends.

drills.name: Ten-second overview
drills.instructions: Look at an image and produce only a one- or two-sentence overview in no more than ten seconds. Include the image type, topic, and dominant pattern.

drills.name: Highest–lowest–difference
drills.instructions: For bar charts, tables, and pie charts, identify the highest value, lowest value, and one meaningful comparison, then speak for 20 seconds using accurate figures.

drills.name: Trend verb ladder
drills.instructions: Describe the same movement using several accurate expressions, such as 'rose,' 'increased steadily,' 'grew sharply,' 'reached a peak,' and 'remained stable.'

drills.name: Photo contrast pairs
drills.instructions: Choose three pairs of contrasting adjectives, such as old and new, high and low, rough and smooth, or traditional and modern, and build a 30-second photograph description.

drills.name: Process sequencing
drills.instructions: Describe a six-stage process using 'first,' 'after this,' 'next,' 'then,' and 'finally.' Repeat the description with fewer pauses on the second attempt.

drills.name: Information-word stress
drills.instructions: Read a model response aloud and underline key nouns, adjectives, verbs, and numbers. Repeat it while stressing those words and reducing small grammatical words.

drills.name: Fluency ladder
drills.instructions: Describe one image three times: first for 20 seconds, then 30 seconds, and finally 40 seconds. Add useful details each time without increasing speaking speed.

drills.name: No-restart challenge
drills.instructions: Record a response and continue speaking even after a minor mistake. Use a linker to recover instead of returning to the beginning.

drills.name: Peer checklist
drills.instructions: One learner speaks while a partner checks the overview, relevant content, organization, tense, vocabulary, fluency, stress, pronunciation, and intonation. The partner gives one specific strength and one actionable improvement.

practice_plan.routine: For each practice image, spend 25 seconds creating six keyword notes, record one response of up to 40 seconds, listen once without stopping, score the response for content, fluency, and pronunciation, write one correction target, and record the same image again while applying only that target. Complete three to five images per study session and rotate among statistical, spatial, and process visuals.

mastery_checklist: I can state that Describe Image provides 25 seconds for preparation and 40 seconds for speaking.
I can identify the image type and main topic within the first five seconds of preparation.
I can read titles, labels, legends, dates, axes, units, and captions accurately.
I can create a six-note plan without writing complete sentences.
I can begin with an overview instead of an isolated number or minor detail.
I can select the highest-value information rather than attempting to describe everything.
I can support major observations with accurate figures, labels, stages, or visible evidence.
I can organize graphs by time, ranking, category, or trend.
I can organize photographs by contrast or spatial position.
I can organize process diagrams from the first stage to the final outcome.
I can choose present, past, or projection language from the image's time information.
I can use approximation language when an exact value is not clearly visible.
I can speak in connected sense groups rather than pausing after individual words.
I can maintain a natural, controlled pace for approximately 35 to 40 seconds.
I can stress key nouns, adjectives, verbs, dates, numbers, and contrast markers.
I can pronounce percentages, large numbers, dates, and measurement units clearly.
I can recover from a minor mistake without restarting my response.
I can finish with a brief overall observation when time permits.
I can evaluate my recording for content, oral fluency, and pronunciation.
I can identify one specific improvement and apply it in a second recording.
strategy_notes: Treat the preparation period as decision-making time, not sentence-writing time.
A strong response is selective: two or three well-supported features are better than a long list of disconnected details.
The overview should explain the visual's subject and dominant message before specific evidence is introduced.
For charts without a clear trend, use a predictable route such as left to right, highest to lowest, or largest to smallest.
For pie charts, begin with the largest segment and group smaller related segments when useful.
For photographs, describe the central subject or main contrast first, then add spatially organized evidence.
For processes, focus on sequence and transformation rather than trying to explain causes that are not shown.
When a number is difficult to read, use careful approximation rather than inventing precision.
Do not spend valuable time on decorative details, source notes, or tiny labels unless they affect the main interpretation.
Use short linking expressions to maintain flow, but avoid filling the response with empty memorized phrases.
Grammar should be controlled but not unnecessarily complex; accurate simple and compound sentences support better fluency.
A brief silent breath before recording can help establish a controlled pace and a clear opening.
Do not wait for a perfect first sentence. Start with a reliable overview structure and develop the response from the plan.
Practise number groups separately, including percentages, years, decimals, fractions, millions, and comparisons.
Recordings should be reviewed for audible features, not only transcript accuracy: listen for pace, pauses, stress, endings, and clarity.
Peer feedback should be specific, such as 'stress the figures more clearly' or 'add one comparison,' rather than general comments such as 'speak better.'
During repeated practice, change only one or two performance targets at a time so improvement can be measured.
Fluency does not mean speaking as quickly as possible; it means maintaining smooth, intelligible, and appropriately phrased speech.
A short accurate ending is useful, but continuing with unsupported filler merely to reach 40 seconds can weaken the response.
The best reusable framework is a flexible speaking order, not a fixed paragraph that ignores the actual image.
